newsitem.title: ALBANIA: New Albania cabinet takes office, pledges security.
newsitem.headline: New Albania cabinet takes office, pledges security.

text.p: Albania's new Socialist Party government took office on Friday, vowing to restore security to the lawless nation after five months of chaos.

The new ministers led by Socialist party chairman Fatos Nano took the oath of office before new president Rexhep Mejdani at the Palace of Brigades, the former villa of the late King Zog on a hillside outside Tirana.

"We shall restore order very soon, within weeks we shall restore security on the national roads and within a few months all around the country, in the towns, everywhere," said new Interior Minister Neritan Ceka.
"We shall apply the law very strictly and we shall also have international support."
The new cabinet went immediately into its first meeting.

Mejdani, a former physics professor who joined the Socialist Party only last year, was elected by the parliament on Thursday and immediately asked Nano as the leader of the parliamentary majority to form a cabinet.

Albania has been ruled by a Socialist-led national unity government since March, when former president Sali Berisha's Democratic Party government stepped down at the height of unrest sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.
Outgoing interim prime minister Bashkim Fino becomes deputy premier in the new lineup, while interim finance minister Arben Malaj retains his post.
Paskal Milo, a history professor and deputy leader of the Social Democratic Party, the Socialists' main coalition allies, becomes foreign minister.
Economy Minister Ylli Bufi, a Socialist, was premier in a 1991 national unity government. Ceka, an archaeologist, is leader of the Democratic Alliance, another coalition partner.

Berisha resigned as president on Wednesday, shortly before the new parliament met for the first time. The legislature lifted the state of emergency and curfew on Thursday and elected Mejdani, news greeted with celebratory volleys of gunfire late into Thursday night.
Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro urged Mejdani to continue rapidly along the path to democracy and pledged his country's continued solidarity.
"Italy fervently hopes Albania can rapidly conclude its processes of normalisation and consolidation of democratic institutions," Scalfaro said in his message.
Italy leads a 7,000-strong international security force in Albania which began withdrawing last week, leaving armed gangs as the sole authority in many areas particularly in the south.
At least three people were killed and 16 injured by an explosion which destroyed three floors of an apartment block in the northeastern town of Peshkopi early on Friday, the Interior Ministry said.
Explosives and weapons were looted from arms depots during the unrest and are frequently used to settle personal disputes.

Nano is expected to present his cabinet's programme to parliament on Monday for a confidence vote from the assembly, in which the Socialists and their coalition allies have 119 of the 155 seats, while Berisha's Democrats have 27.
The Democrats are boycotting the assembly to protest at the conditions in which the elections were held.

Apart from restoring security, Nano's main task will be to sort out the economic chaos left by the collapse of high-interest pyramid schemes and put Europe's poorest country on the road to reconstruction and modernisation.
His party campaigned in part on a promise to compensate pyramid investors who lost their life savings early this year -- a promise its opponents are unlikely to let it escape.

Nano, 44, who had been jailed on corruption charges that his Socialists say were politically motivated, insists his reformed party has nothing to do with the Stalinist regime of Enver Hoxha who ruled for 40 years until his death in 1985.
Hoxha's successor, communist president Ramiz Alia, ruled out change but anti-government protests from July 1990 led to reforms culminating in multi-party elections in March 1991.
